items.stem: A homologous series is a family of compounds that:
choices: Share a general formula and functional group, successive members differing by CH₂
items.note: Definition question — the CH₂ increment explains the gradual boiling-point trends within a series.

items.stem: The compound CH₃CH₂CHO is classified as:
items.note: –CHO at the end of a chain = aldehyde (propanal). A C=O inside the chain would make it a ketone (propanone).

items.stem: The correct IUPAC name for CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is:
items.note: Longest chain = 4 carbons (butane); a methyl on carbon 2. Number from the end giving the lowest locant — always check both directions.

items.stem: How many structural isomers does C₄H₁₀ have?
items.note: Butane and 2-methylpropane. Isomers = same molecular formula, different arrangement of atoms.

items.stem: Bromine water is decolorized rapidly by:
items.note: The C=C double bond adds Br₂ across itself — the standard test: unsaturated decolorizes, saturated stays orange.

items.stem: Butan-2-ol is classified as a:
items.note: The carbon bearing –OH is attached to two other carbons → secondary. This matters because oxidation products differ by class.

items.stem: Oxidation of butan-2-ol with an acidified oxidant gives:
items.note: Secondary alcohols oxidize to ketones — and ketones resist further oxidation. Primary → aldehyde → acid; tertiary resist.

items.stem: To obtain an aldehyde (rather than the carboxylic acid) from the oxidation of a primary alcohol, you should:
choices: Distil the aldehyde out as it forms
items.note: Distil immediately so the aldehyde leaves the mixture before further oxidation; reflux with excess oxidant drives it to the acid.

items.stem: Converting a halogenoalkane to an alcohol using aqueous NaOH is an example of:
items.note: OH⁻ is the nucleophile — it donates a pair to the electron-poor C–X carbon, replacing the halogen. Polar C–X bond enables this.

items.stem: Heating a halogenoalkane with KOH dissolved in ethanol produces mainly:
items.note: Same reagent, different solvent = different reaction: aqueous OH⁻ substitutes, ethanolic OH⁻ eliminates (loss of HX). Solvent decides the outcome.

items.stem: The product of the reaction between ethene and HBr is:
items.note: Addition across the double bond: H and Br add to the two carbons → bromoethane. (Br₂ would give 1,2-dibromoethane.)

items.stem: Poly(ethene) is formed from ethene by:
choices: Condensation polymerization with loss of water
Addition polymerization of C=C double bonds
items.note: Alkene double bonds open and link into saturated chains. Addition polymers have the same empirical formula as the monomer.

items.stem: An ester is formed from the reaction of:
choices: A carboxylic acid and an alcohol with an acid catalyst
items.note: Esterification: acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water, warm with acid catalyst. Esters' distinctive smells are the classic identification clue.

items.stem: Burning methane in a limited oxygen supply produces the toxic gas:
items.note: Incomplete combustion → carbon monoxide (and soot). Complete combustion needs plenty of oxygen: CO₂ + H₂O only.

items.stem: The halogenation of methane with chlorine requires ultraviolet light. The UV light:
choices: Provides the activation energy for ionic substitution
Initiates the formation of free radicals
items.note: UV homolytically splits Cl₂ into Cl· radicals — initiation. Propagation steps then continue a chain reaction; termination pairs radicals.

items.stem: An infrared spectrum of an unknown pure compound shows a broad absorption at 3200–3600 cm⁻¹. The compound likely contains:
items.note: Broad ~3200–3600 cm⁻¹ = O–H (alcohol/acid); sharp strong ~1700 cm⁻¹ = C=O. IR gives functional groups, not structure.

items.stem: Which statement about benzene is correct?
choices: It readily adds bromine across its ring
Its bonds are alternating long-short single/double bonds
It reacts by substitution, preserving the delocalized π system
It is classified as an alkene
items.note: Delocalized π electrons stabilize the ring — equal C–C bond lengths (bond order ~1.5) and substitution (not addition) reactivity.

items.stem: Branched alkanes have lower boiling points than their straight-chain isomers because branching:
choices: Reduces surface contact → weaker London forces between molecules
items.note: Same formula, same covalent bonds — only the packing changes. Straight chains touch along their length; branched ones can't.

items.stem: Which reaction type converts propene into propan-2-ol as the major product?
choices: Addition of water across the double bond (hydration)
Oxidation with acidified permanganate at room temperature
items.note: Hydration of the asymmetric alkene follows Markovnikov's rule (HL): OH adds to the carbon with fewer hydrogens → propan-2-ol major.

items.stem: The general formula of the alkene homologous series (acyclic, one double bond) is:
items.note: Alkenes CₙH₂ₙ (one degree of unsaturation vs alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂). Useful for deducing formulas from spectra or combustion data.

items.stem: Draw and name the structural isomers of C₄H₈O that contain a carbonyl group (aldehydes and ketones only).
items.tactic: Isomer problems: fix the formula, fix the functional group, then systematically move the position and branch the chain. Missing one isomer is the usual mark loss.

items.stem: State the reagents and conditions to convert propene into propanone in two steps, naming each organic product.
markscheme: Step 1: hydrate propene — steam/H₃PO₄ catalyst → propan-2-ol (major, Markovnikov) (2: reagents 1, product 1)
Step 2: oxidize propan-2-ol — acidified dichromate, heat → propanone (secondary alcohol → ketone) (2: reagents 1, product 1)
Overall logic: addition then oxidation, via the secondary alcohol (1)
items.tactic: Two-step synthesis: work backwards from the target (ketone ← secondary alcohol ← alkene). Name every intermediate — unnamed steps lose marks.
